description_full: Casey's General Stores, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates convenience stores under the Casey's and Casey's General Store names in the United States. Its stores offer pizza, donuts, hot breakfast items, and sandwiches; and beverages, tobacco and nicotine products. The company's stores also provide soft drinks, energy, water, sports drinks, juices, coffee, and tea and dairy products; beer, wine, and spirits; snacks, candy, packaged bakery, and other food items; ice, ice cream, meals, and appetizers; health and beauty aids, automotive products, electronic accessories, and housewares. In addition, its stores offer motor fuel for sale on a self-service basis; gasoline and diesel fuel; and ATM, lotto/lottery, and prepaid cards, as well as car wash services. The company also operates distribution centers. Casey's General Stores, Inc. was founded in 1959 and is headquartered in Ankeny, Iowa.

financial_summary: Caseys General Stores, Inc. is a large-cap consumer cyclical business with a $26.3B market cap on $17.6B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +5% over the past three years and +9% annually across the full decade, a respectable pace for a business of this size.

Returns on capital run at 9% against a 8% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically, and 20% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $722M in free cash flow — roughly 4 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.93× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 4.2× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and interest coverage runs at 9.7×.
Shareholder yield is only 1.1%, a thin return of capital, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+22.2% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 20% over the past year excluding the latest month, though it has pulled back 17% over the last three months.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 23% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 38% and a beta of 0.64, it is more defensive than the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $325.9M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 33% in the 2020 crash, 16% in the 2022 bear market and 39% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $555 (margin of safety -28%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 52%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $380 to $819 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 34.3 vs 18.8, EV/EBITDA 18.2 vs 10.7 and P/FCF 36.5 vs 16.7 (sector median).
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.7% (below the risk-free rate).
The 19 covering analysts target $789 on average, 11% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
The price implies 16.1% annual cash-flow growth, 4pp more than the model expects.
prof: ROIC of 9% earns above the cost of capital of 7.6%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have been steady (CV 0.15).
It runs a 20% gross margin and converts 4% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.93x.
ROE of 18% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.3x equity multiplier).
It spends 0.4% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 4.2x net debt to EBITDA ($523.0M of cash against $2.4B of debt), with interest covered 9.7x.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 5.2% over 3 years, 15.1% over 5 years and 9.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating, and it has been lumpy (year-to-year swings of 14%).
Free cash flow has compounded 14.7% a year over five years.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (1.5x, 3.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 19, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 15.8% on average.
Analysts expect 10.0% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and institutions hold 91%.
Insider trading is two-way: 1 purchase and 29 sales over the past year, net $31.3M sold.
Shareholder yield is a modest 1.1% (0.8% in buybacks and 0.4% in dividends).
It has paid a dividend for 35 consecutive years, raising it 11.6% a year over the last five.
people: With about 23,490 employees, each generates about $748K of revenue, 2.0x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 7.9% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $31K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $5.1M (7x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
